deck.title: Big Leap DIY Toolkits: Live Sales Demo Deck

note: Internal. Value points avoid pricing and promises of results; proof points carry their source. "heard" lines are patterns from real discovery calls, generalized and anonymized — never a specific client's name. Edit here, then rebuild the deck requests with tools/build_sales_deck.py.

start.headline: Start with your business, not a pitch.
points: Eight questions build a Business Profile that fills in every other toolkit.
The result points to the service to start with, in your own words.
Nothing is stored on Big Leap's side. Answers stay in your browser.
start.ask: Before I show you anything, let's answer a few questions about the business together.
start.listen: What they sell, where customers come from, which CRM they use, and how many locations they have.
start.next: Use the result to pick which service section of this deck to open next.

services.name: RevOps
services.story: Most small businesses can't say which lead became which customer — so every budget call after that is a guess, and the whole thing runs on whichever person remembers to follow up.
value: Every form, call and chat lands in the CRM with its source attached.
Fast, automatic follow-up, with a named owner on every lead.
Reporting that ties marketing spend to pipeline and closed revenue.
heard: “We're basically on a wild goose chase every time someone asks for a case status.” — a common line when leads are scattered across tools with no single source of truth.
The business runs on one person's memory. If they're out sick, new leads stall.
A CRM holding thousands of contacts, with only a small fraction of them actually active or current.

proof.text: Companies that tried to reach a new lead within an hour were 7x as likely to qualify it as those that waited longer, and over 60x as likely as those that waited 24 hours or more.
proof.source: Harvard Business Review, The Short Life of Online Sales Leads (2011)

proof.text: Only 56% of marketers have complete access to sales data. High performers are 2.4x more likely to have unified their data sources.

options.headline: Put a number on hand work.
points: Turns copy-paste, data entry and manual follow-up into hours per month.
That number makes the case for automation in your own terms.
Hours back go to selling instead of updating records.
options.ask: Walk me through everything that happens between a new lead and a booked meeting.
options.listen: Manual steps: copying leads between tools, reminders, re-keying data, chasing status.
options.next: We automate the repeatable steps in the CRM and hand the hours back to the team.

options.headline: Reply before they move on.
points: One minute shows whether new leads wait hours for a first reply.
An automatic first reply buys time while a person follows up.
A named owner on every lead means nothing slips through.
options.ask: When a form comes in at 4:45 on a Friday, what happens next?
options.listen: "Same day" or later, no automatic reply, or "whoever sees it first."
options.next: We set up instant replies, routing and owner alerts in the CRM so every lead hears back fast.

options.headline: Know what your marketing actually does.
points: Checks whether leads, calls and sales trace back to the channel that drove them.
Gaps here mean budget decisions are made on guesswork.
Most businesses score lower than they expect, which opens the conversation.
options.ask: If I asked which channel brought in last month's best customer, could you show me?
options.listen: "Not sure", spreadsheets, or different answers from marketing and sales.
options.next: We connect forms, calls, ads and the CRM into one view from source to revenue.

services.name: Paid Media
services.story: Too many ad accounts run on autopilot — the same creative as last year, sometimes the same ad copy as a direct competitor — with nobody checking whether the budget is still working.
value: Account structure and tracking fixed before budget scales.
Bidding trained on leads and sales that matter, including offline results.
Campaign choices matched to the goal, demand and budget.
heard: “We paid about five thousand a month for six to eight months and got zero leads.” It's what happens when nobody reviews the account.
“Our last agency used the exact same ad copy for us and for our direct competitor.”
Budget keeps renewing because cancelling feels riskier than the status quo — even when nobody can say what it's actually producing.

proof.text: Google reports that advertisers who moved from target CPA to target ROAS (value-based bidding) saw conversion value rise 14% on average.
proof.source: Google, Think with Google (2022, Google internal data)

proof.text: In one Google case study, retailer MandM Direct saw 3% more conversions on Search and 20% more on YouTube after setting up enhanced conversions. Results vary.

options.headline: Put a number on a messy account.
points: One minute turns "not sure" about tracking into a monthly dollar range.
Ties back to Google's own published lift from fixing the signal, not a guess.
A number a business owner can act on before paying for management.
options.ask: If I asked what Google counts as a conversion in your account right now, could you tell me?
options.listen: "Not sure", clicks or page views, or an account nobody's reviewed in months.
options.next: We audit the account, fix tracking and structure, then show the number again.

options.headline: Ready before you spend.
points: Spots the setup gaps that waste budget in the first weeks.
Shows what to fix before paying for clicks, or for management.
Gives a clear starting point instead of a vague audit.
options.ask: Who set up your Google Ads account, and when did someone last review it end to end?
options.listen: An old setup, a past agency, or "we just boost what's working."
options.next: We audit and fix the account foundation first, then scale what works.

options.headline: Teach your ads what a customer is.
points: Shows whether Google optimizes for real leads or for clicks and page views.
Counting the wrong action trains bidding to find more of the wrong people.
Feeding CRM results back lets bidding learn from actual sales.
options.ask: What does Google Ads count as a conversion in your account today?
options.listen: Page views, button clicks, "all form fills", or nobody is sure.
options.next: We set up conversion tracking, values and CRM imports so bidding learns from sales.

options.headline: Start with the right campaign.
points: Matches the goal, demand and budget to the first campaign worth running.
Avoids spreading a small budget across too many campaign types.
Builds a base of data the next campaigns can learn from.
options.ask: If you could only run one campaign next month, what would it need to achieve?
options.listen: Leads versus sales versus awareness, the monthly budget, and how many people search for what they sell.
options.next: We build the first campaign around that goal, then expand as the data comes in.

services.name: SEO
services.story: A lot of SEO pain shows up after a migration nobody checked, or a plateau nobody explained — and now AI tools are a second search engine most sites haven't shown up in yet.
value: Technical health that lets Google and AI tools crawl and trust the site.
A local presence that is complete and consistent: Business Profile, listings, reviews.
Content and authority built on that foundation.
heard: A migration can quietly leave thousands of broken pages and open redirects behind — the kind of thing a past agency never mentions.
Rankings that slide from the teens into single digits over a year, while the invoices keep arriving.
Twenty reviews sitting next to a competitor's two or three hundred.

proof.text: 97% of consumers read online reviews, 89% expect the owner to respond, and 45% now use ChatGPT or other AI tools for local recommendations (up from 6%).
When a Google AI summary appeared, people clicked a regular search result in 8% of visits, versus 15% without one.

options.headline: Put a number on being invisible to AI search.
points: Turns "haven't checked" into a monthly range of visits that could be at risk.
Ties to Google and Pew's own published AI-summary click-through data, not a guess.
A fast way into the AI-visibility conversation without the jargon.
options.ask: When you ask ChatGPT or Google's AI about your category, does your business come up?
options.listen: "I've never checked", or a competitor named instead of them.
options.next: We check the foundation, then build the content and authority AI tools cite.

options.headline: Findable by Google and AI search.
points: Checks crawling, indexing and the trust signals search engines and AI tools rely on.
Problems here cap the return on every other SEO investment.
A quick way to bring up AI search visibility without the jargon.
options.ask: When you ask ChatGPT or Google's AI about your category, does your business come up?
options.listen: "I've never checked", or competitors named instead of them.
options.next: We fix the foundation, then build the content and authority that AI and search tools cite.

options.headline: Get found nearby.
points: Checks the Business Profile, listing consistency and local pages.
The map results are often the first thing a local searcher sees.
Works per location, so multi-location brands see every gap.
options.ask: Search "[your service] near me" from your phone. Where do you show up?
options.listen: Missing from the map, wrong hours or phone number, or one location stronger than the rest.
options.next: We manage profiles, listings and local pages for every location.

options.headline: Reviews people trust.
points: Reads review count, recency and replies at a glance.
Recent reviews with owner replies help a profile earn the click.
Turns reputation into a routine instead of a scramble.
options.ask: How do you ask customers for reviews today, and who replies to them?
options.listen: No routine, old reviews, or negative reviews left without a reply.
options.next: We set up a steady review-request and reply process across your locations.

services.name: Digital PR
services.story: The fear usually isn't bad press — it's losing control of the story before a journalist, a review site or an AI summary tells it first.
value: Expert positioning and story angles journalists actually use.
Coverage and links from publications your buyers trust.
A media kit and spokesperson ready before the pitch goes out.
heard: Worry that one bad review, a lawsuit mention or an old news story becomes the AI-generated summary of the business.
Wanting to get ahead of the narrative, not clean one up after the fact.

proof.text: 66% of journalists rely on PR-provided content for story ideas. They want original research, expert access and embargoed information.
58% of Americans 12 and older (167 million) listened to a podcast in the last month, an all-time high.
proof.source: Edison Research and SSRS, The Infinite Dial (2026)

options.headline: Ready before the story gets told without you.
points: Checks the spokesperson, story angles and proof points before pitching starts.
Journalists and AI summaries both move fast — being ready is the difference between shaping the story and reacting to it.
Shows what you need to bring to a PR program.
options.ask: If a reporter — or an AI tool summarizing your industry — needed a quote from you tomorrow, who would it be?
options.listen: No named spokesperson, no data or stories ready, or a slow approvals process.
options.next: We shape the angles, prep the spokesperson and pitch the right outlets.

options.headline: Make it easy to quote you.
points: Checks the bio, headshots, company facts and past coverage a journalist expects.
A ready kit shortens the path from pitch to published story.
Useful well beyond press: partners, podcasts and events ask for the same things.
options.ask: Where would a journalist find your founder's bio and a usable headshot today?
options.listen: Scattered files, outdated bios, or "we'd have to put that together."
options.next: We build and maintain the media kit alongside every campaign.

options.headline: Ready for the mic.
points: Checks topics, story and audience fit before pitching yourself as a guest.
Podcasts give long-form time with exactly the right audience.
Pairs with an invite to pitch Big Leap's Sweet Takes podcast. Asking doesn't book a spot.
options.ask: What could you talk about for 30 minutes that your best customers would want to hear?
options.listen: A clear point of view, customer stories, or a founder who enjoys talking.
options.next: We find shows that fit, prep the talking points, and handle the pitching.

services.name: Email Marketing
services.story: Email is the channel you own outright — but only if it reaches the inbox and sends at the moment someone actually cares.
value: Deliverability set up right: authentication, unsubscribe and list hygiene.
Automated flows that send at the moment of intent: welcome, follow-up, win-back.
Results measured in revenue and leads, not just opens.

proof.text: Automated flows drive nearly 41% of email revenue from 5.3% of sends, with revenue per recipient nearly 18x higher than campaigns.
Since February 2024, bulk senders to Gmail and Yahoo must authenticate with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, offer one-click unsubscribe, and keep spam complaints under 0.3%.

options.headline: Put a number on a list with no flows.
points: Turns "we only send a newsletter" into a monthly revenue range.
Built on Klaviyo's own published flow-vs-campaign benchmark, not a guess.
Shows which flow is worth building first, before writing a single email.
options.ask: What email does a new subscriber or customer get from you in their first week?
options.listen: Nothing, a single receipt, or only the monthly newsletter.
options.next: We plan, write, build and test the flows in your email platform.

options.headline: Keep reaching the inbox.
points: Checks the authentication, unsubscribe and complaint basics Gmail and Yahoo require of bulk senders.
Missing them can push mail to spam or get it rejected.
A fast, concrete check most senders haven't done.
options.ask: Have you set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the domain you send from?
options.listen: "What's that?", "IT handled it years ago", or open rates that dropped suddenly.
options.next: We set up authentication and list hygiene, then keep an eye on deliverability.

options.headline: Emails that send themselves.
points: Finds the automated emails a business is missing.
Flows send at the moment of intent, every time, without extra work.
Usually the fastest email win for a team that only sends newsletters.
options.ask: What email does a new subscriber or customer get from you in their first week?
options.listen: Nothing, a single receipt, or only the monthly newsletter.
options.next: We plan, write, build and test the flows in your email platform.

options.headline: A one-minute health check.
points: Reads complaints, list hygiene and results in one view.
Small problems compound: a dirty list hurts every future send.
A clear before-and-after for renewals and audits.
options.ask: When did you last remove subscribers who haven't opened in six months or more?
options.listen: Never, a list that keeps growing while results fall, or rising complaints.
options.next: We run regular audits and fix issues before they cost revenue.

services.name: Strategy
services.story: Most businesses aren't missing a tactic. They're missing someone who owns the whole picture instead of one more vendor adding to the pile.
value: Diagnose the real constraint before choosing channels.
Reuse what already works instead of starting over.
Build a brand and customer experience worth recommending.
heard: “We don't want the rigid-retainer agency flow — we want a real partner.”
A two- or three-person team trying to keep marketing running across dozens of locations.
A handful of vendors, each doing their own piece, and nobody owning how they fit together.

proof.text: Recommendations from people they know are the most trusted source of advertising: 89% of US consumers trust them.
73% of B2B decision-makers trust peer recommendations, more than vendor websites (55%) or search engines (54%). The study was sponsored by Reddit.
proof.source: Reddit and SurveyMonkey, The Hidden B2B Journey (2026)

options.headline: Find the one problem actually worth solving.
points: Two questions point to where marketing should focus right now, not whichever tactic came up last.
Keeps the conversation on the real constraint, not whichever vendor pitched most recently.
A natural opener for any service conversation.
options.ask: If marketing went perfectly for the next year, what would be different for the business?
options.listen: Not enough demand, demand that doesn't convert, or customers who don't stick.
options.next: We turn the answer into a prioritized plan and the first services to start with.

options.headline: Fix the foundation first.
points: Four checks show which foundation everything else depends on.
Reuses what you already have instead of starting over.
Puts the work in the order it pays off.
options.ask: What do you already have that's working, even a little?
options.listen: A brand guide nobody uses, a site that converts poorly, or tracking nobody trusts.
options.next: We scope the work in order: foundation first, then growth.

options.headline: Worth recommending.
points: Three habits that turn customers into reviews and referrals.
Recommendations from people they know are among the sources buyers trust most.
Strong for retention, renewals and post-sale check-ins.
options.ask: When a happy customer finishes working with you, what happens next?
options.listen: Nothing formal, no review ask, or referrals that happen by luck.
options.next: We build follow-up, review and referral moments into the customer journey.
